issues: The 7-step pipeline maps each phase to a skill clearly, but steps 1 and 2 conflict on order. senior-architect runs 'before feature work', while github-issue-lifecycle must start 'every code-change request... before reading or editing code'. The file doesn't say whether architecture work gets its own issue.

Step 4 says to load senior-qa/api-test-suite-builder 'before the spec's test plan and again before the tests', but step 5 (tdd-guide) also owns writing tests. It's unclear which skill decides test content.
'Rarely self-trigger; load:' is hard to read. It's unclear whether these skills are on-demand only or should load automatically when the listed condition appears (flaky tests, migrations, etc.).

'With no possible user turn (a scheduled job, not `-p`)' is confusing. It suggests `-p` runs can still ask questions, which isn't true for most headless invocations, and it doesn't say how to detect which case applies.
The overlay fallback path `~/.claude/skill-overlays/<full skill name>.md` can't be checked from here. There is no rule for what to do if both the injected overlay and the file are missing.
The skills it names (senior-architect, ship-gate, focused-fix, skill-tester, etc.) aren't checked for existence, and nothing says what to do if one isn't installed. That's a currency risk.

Some rules repeat or overlap. The 'one adversarial pass' rule shows up in Pipeline step 6, in Reviews ('one pass on the full diff'), and in No-review mode. 'A change to an approved spec re-enters its mode' repeats the manual-mode line 'Any change after approval... returns it to draft'.
The rules on approval-mode conflicts ('manual review beats no review; else the more specific statement wins') don't cover how Adversarial approval ranks against the other two modes.

'Never re-run it, even after fixes or a CRITICAL' with 'A later change for another reason gets its own pass' leaves the boundary unclear. A fix for a CRITICAL is a change, so it's ambiguous whether it counts as 'another reason'.

Some rules are too terse to apply as written. One example is 'Gates add to the user's authority and never stand in for it'. Another is the coordinator/fork approval labeling in a split, where the manual-mode text says the coordinator applies labels but the Splitting section says forks own everything through the PR.

The tests/lint/typecheck rule has no fallback for when a project defines none of them. It also doesn't point to the project CLAUDE.md for the actual commands, only saying in general that project files win.
Few rules explain why they exist (no squash, semantic-release-only tags, the `python3 -I` literal-path rule). That makes edge cases harder to judge.
